there was a market maker, one of the G10 crosses

spent all his time watching nature videos. I asked my boss how he never got fired bc the guy seemed completely cooked. He spent all day screaming on the loud speakers and bothering 1rst year analysts / coming up w strange / inappropriate names for people 

"In the GFC, that guy made so much money that it might have prevented the firm from going bankrupt"

I walked up to him. "Can you tell me about how you made so much money in 08"

After a brief paroxysm of calling an analyst a vulgar name, he motions for me to sit in front of him

"Here's how it went. You see, the US dollar. It would always pancake. Nobody wanted US dollars. The story was all overseas. Every corporate, every fund, sell only.

It would pancaaaake. 

But one day, the dollar stopped pancaking.

I could smell that it wasn't going to pancake anymore. So I bought $1 billion. 

Within 30 minutes clients had already taken me out of the position so I bought another $1b and so on

It was a blur. I realized that no many dollars I was buying clients kept coming in and taking me out of my inventory

I decided that if it had spent so long pancaking a lot of people who were betting it would pancake, would have their funds pancaked

I bought so many dollars the CEO of the bank came to my desk and asked me what I was seeing. I explained to him that the dollar always pancaked, but it had stopped pancaking. And that people didn't want dollars. They *needed* dollars. 

He looked pretty grim but asked me what I needed to do. I told him I needed to buy more dollars. So I did."

I asked him how he decided to stop buying dollars.

He paused. "One day, the government came in and basically told everyone they were going to supply dollars in infinite size. So it was back to pancaking. I sold all my dollars and am only short the dollar ever since"

the moral of the story? honestly, there isn't one. The guy didn't really do well financially. He worked a huge amount, and I don't think his family appreciated that. He made the bank huge amounts of money but I'm pretty sure whatever bonus he got was offset from massive financial losses owning the company's stock.

Maybe there's one lesson. Things pancake. Until they don't.

Stablecoin issuers may be solving the wrong problem.

@OpenStandard argues that issuers make most of their money from reserve income, so they have less incentive to optimize for transactions.

Fair point.

Though, I would say that the more difficult problems are usually operational:

→ Accounting treatment is still messy
→ Compliance adds extra work
→ Moving between stablecoins and fiat is still clunky
→ Payment tracking is still messy
→ Treasury teams need extra infrastructure

USDT and USDC already move huge amounts of money even though their issuers keep most of the revenue from reserves.

So the traditional business model clearly doesn’t prevent stablecoins from being used.

Sharing more of the economics with businesses might help distribution, but it doesn’t solve the operational mess around the token.

This is still the bigger bottleneck if you ask me.

Tokenization can make the same equity available across several crypto venues, but that does not make those markets equally liquid.

That difference showed up in a July 16 test of a $100K tokenized NVDA purchase. During US market hours, the test found a 24x spread in slippage between Jupiter and Bybit. A trader could therefore pay far more for the same stock exposure simply by choosing a different venue.

But the price gap tells only part of the story. Bybit was cheaper because one large resting order absorbed almost the entire purchase. On Binance, the same trade moved through 53 smaller orders at progressively higher prices. Bybit delivered the better price, while Binance’s liquidity was distributed more broadly across its order book.

Time mattered as well. Trading continued after the US market closed, but execution became more expensive on both centralized venues. Bybit’s advantage narrowed as the front of its order book thinned, while the onchain route remained consistently expensive.

Two order-book snapshots cannot establish a permanent venue ranking. They do illustrate the larger challenge: tokenization can make an equity accessible in more places, but every venue must still build the depth and resilience needed to trade it efficiently.

⚡ THE DAILY METALS PULSE | 11 SEPTEMBER 2026 ⚡
Four metals. One pulse. No noise.

CPI delivered the expected inflation shock.

US consumer prices rose 0.4% in August, with core inflation increasing 0.3%. Markets now price an 87% probability of a Fed hike next week.

But something interesting happened after the initial selloff:

Gold and silver reversed higher.

☢️ URANIUM

Numerco’s latest public physical OTC U₃O₈ indication remains around $90/lb.

A separate benchmark-linked financial reference increased to $90.20. That is not a completed physical spot transaction, and neither price should be confused with uranium miners or listed trusts.

As the World Nuclear Symposium concludes, the conversation is shifting from whether nuclear will expand to how that expansion will be financed.

The uranium move remains intact. Fresh physical transactions must now confirm it.

🟠 COPPER

Copper is around $6.47/lb, while three-month LME copper has retreated toward $14,250 per tonne after reaching a record $14,875.

The trigger was political, not geological.

Washington’s hesitation over refined-copper tariffs rapidly removed the premium created by metal being redirected into US warehouses.

Copper may end its ten-week winning streak, but no new mines appeared during the selloff. The structural supply problem remains.

🥈 SILVER

Silver has rebounded approximately 1.6% to $64.50/oz, although it remains down around 2.6% this week.

Higher rates and copper’s reversal destroyed the breakout. Dip-buying after CPI prevented the decline from accelerating.

Silver has not regained momentum, but it has shown that investors are willing to defend it near $63–64.

🥇 GOLD

Gold has recovered approximately 1.1% to $4,363/oz despite the probability of a September rate hike rising to 87%.

That is the day’s most important signal.

Gold initially fell on inflation and higher yields. Buyers then stepped in while the US 10-year yield remained near 4.93%.

The market is still treating inflation as a reason for tighter policy. But gold’s reversal suggests investors are also beginning to remember why hard assets exist.

Hot CPI.
Near-certain rate hike.
Gold and silver still reversed higher.

The hard-asset trade took a hit this week.
It did not disappear.

94.4% of FOMO traders lost money over the last 60 days. You just don’t see those screenshots.

Memecoins are high risk and high reward, but you can lower the risk by following a checklist:

• Liquidity. Market cap tells you almost nothing here. Look at how much money is actually sitting in the pool. If your position is already meaningful compared with the liquidity, getting out can get ugly fast.

• Supply concentration. Check top holders, bundled buys and wallet funding. A launch can look organic while a few connected wallets already control most of the supply.

• Who buys after you? If the token already did 10x and every large account is posting it, ask who's supposed to buy your bags higher.

• What happens when a whale sells? Thin liquidity plus a few big holders is a horrible combination. One large exit turns into everyone racing for the door.

• Copycats. One meme pumps and suddenly there are 30 versions of it. Once attention starts splitting, volume usually follows.

• Don't blindly copy wallets. Seeing a good trader buy is useful information. It doesn't mean you should buy the second their trade shows up on your feed. I'd rather wait and see what they do after the first big pullback.

• Pick the right table. Some meme markets are almost entirely experienced onchain traders playing against each other. Others pull in much broader users. Knowing who you're trading against matters.

$LAPTOP is a clean example of all of this. It crashed almost 97% after launch, and most of the people who bought it were buying someone else's exit without knowing it.

I'm still very open to trading memes when the market gets hot. I just treat them like poker rather than investing.

Figure out who already has the chips and who you expect to buy from you later. Then worry about how much you can make.

I’m not copying anyone’s investment idea. I simply see a very interesting psychological setup that I want to exploit.

I’m not investing in Uber because I think it is the future of mobility. Honestly, I have no idea exactly what the future of mobility will look like.

Uber fell from around $80 to $70 in about a week.

But what actually changed in Uber’s business during that week? Nothing. Only the perception changed.

Nothing Tesla revealed was information that funds like Pershing Square and Appaloosa had not already studied. These people have almost unlimited resources, spoke to every possible expert, and still made Uber one of their largest investments.

Then Uber’s CEO bought $10 million of shares, and its COO bought another $5.3 million. This is less important to me, but it still shows conviction.

So you have what I believe some normal investors dumping the stock because one app became popular, while some of the world’s best investors and Uber’s own management are putting serious money into it.

Maybe they are all wrong. It is possible.
But psychologically, I really like this setup.
